app.title: Lunar Nav Kids — missions to the Moon’s south pole

home.title: Hi! I’m Lumi, your Moon guide.
home.mascotLabel: Lumi, a friendly astronaut robot, waving
home.say1: At the Moon’s south pole the Sun never climbs high: it rolls around the sky, just above the mountains.
home.say2: And the Earth plays hide-and-seek: it bobs up and down and sometimes hides behind the hills.

m1.title: Find the sunniest spot
m1.teaser: Where does the Sun shine the most in July 2030?
m1.intro: A lander needs sunshine for power. Pick a spot and watch the Sun roll along the mountains for 30 days, from 1 July 2030.
m1.sceneLabel: The sky all around {site} on day {day}, with the Sun and the real mountains
m1.mountains: The Sun is hiding behind the mountains.
m1.below: The Sun is below the horizon.
m1.soFar: Sunny days so far: about {n} of {d}.
m1.stripLabel: The 30 days: yellow when the Sun shines (about {n} days in all)
m1.conclusion: The sunniest spot is {best}: about {bestN} of 30 days. The least sunny is {worst}: about {worstN} days.
m1.why: Why? Shackleton’s ridge is high, so the low Sun is almost never blocked. At Malapert, in July 2030, nearby mountains hide the low Sun most of the time.

m2.title: When can we call home?
m2.teaser: Earth bobs up and down and hides behind the hills.
m2.intro: To call home, two things must happen at once: Earth must be above the mountains, and one of NASA’s big antennas on Earth (in California, Spain or Australia) must see the Moon.
m2.sceneLabel: Earth in the sky of {site} on day {day}, with the real mountains
m2.wobble: Earth wobbles up and down between {lo}° and {hi}° (this is called libration).

reason.antennas: Not now: Earth is up, but no antenna on Earth can see the Moon.
reason.mountains: Not now: Earth is hiding behind the mountains.
reason.below: Not now: Earth is below the horizon.

m2.stripLabel: The 30 days: green when you can call home (about {n} days in all)
m2.longest: The longest wait without a call: about {n} days.
m2.longestAtLeast: The longest wait without a call: more than {n} days.
m2.why: The south pole is at the edge of the side of the Moon that faces Earth, so Earth sits low in the sky. A small wobble is enough to hide it.

m3.title: Charge for the long night
m3.teaser: Why does a Moon battery need to be so big?
m3.intro: A night near the Moon’s pole can last for days. With no sunlight the solar panel makes no power, but the lander still needs {load} W to stay warm — like a bright light bulb.
m3.nightDays: The longest night here: about {n} days
m3.nightDaysAtLeast: The longest night here: more than {n} days
m3.nightHours: The longest night here: only about {n} hours
m3.dayText: the solar panel fills the battery up to 100 %.
m3.nightText: the battery gives {load} W all night long. It must last until the Sun comes back.
m3.ranOut: Oh no! The small battery ran out in the middle of the night. The lander gets too cold!
m3.madeIt: Made it! The Sun is back and the battery still has 20 % — just right.
m3.results: How big must the battery be?
m3.battery: About {kwh} kWh — it weighs about {kg} kg!
m3.batteryAtLeast: At least {kwh} kWh — it weighs at least {kg} kg!
m3.batteryTiny: Here the night is so short that a small battery (less than 1 kWh) is enough.
m3.rule: The rule: battery = {load} W × the longest night ÷ 0.8. We only use {dod} % of the battery, so it stays healthy.

scene.taller: The mountains are drawn {n}× taller so you can see them.
scene.sunBigger: The Sun is drawn bigger, too.

shackleton_ridge.about: Shackleton: a high ridge on the rim of Shackleton crater, very close to the south pole.

im2_athena.about: IM-2: where the IM-2 Athena lander touched down in 2025, in the Mons Mouton region.

malapert_m1.about: Malapert: a tall mountain near the south pole.

quiz.title: Moon quiz

questions.q: Which spot had the most sunshine in July 2030?
questions.why: {sunniest} is on a high ridge, so the Sun shines there almost all the time.

questions.q: How does the Sun move in the sky at the Moon’s south pole?
options: It climbs high over our heads
It rolls around the sky, staying low
questions.why: At the pole the Sun stays just above the horizon and goes all the way around.

questions.q: What do we need to call home from the Moon?
options: Earth above the mountains, and a big antenna on Earth that sees the Moon
questions.why: Both are needed at the same time.

questions.q: At IM-2, how long is the longest night?
questions.why: The night there lasts about {night} days.

questions.q: Why does a Moon battery need to be big?
options: To keep the lander warm through the whole long night
To make the lander go faster
questions.why: With no sunlight, the battery must give power until the Sun comes back.

quiz.doneText: Great exploring! Your score is only shown here; it is not saved anywhere.
